methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Science CLIL Integration
content: Problem: Students know words like "rain" or "cloud" but lack the academic vocabulary to explain continuous scientific cycles.

Solution: We explicitly teach the formal scientific terms (evaporation, condensation, precipitation) alongside sequence connectors (First, Then, Next, Finally). This enables students to logically describe a perpetual process using the Present Simple tense.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Session 1: Introduce the 4 stages of the water cycle. Focus on connecting sequence words with the new Tier 1 academic vocabulary.
Session 2: Explore the journey of a raindrop. Practice describing the continuous changes of water states (liquid to gas to liquid).
Session 3: Full production. Write a cohesive scientific report explaining the entire water cycle, and present it orally to the class.

methodology.title: 2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: S1 pull-out: Show a picture of one stage (e.g., rain falling). The student must name the academic term ("That is precipitation!").

Communicative task (Step 5 - 10 min): The Cycle Sorter. Student A has the steps out of order. Student B reads the process using "First, Next...". Student A must arrange the flashcards correctly based on the verbal instructions.

listening_script.text: Hello, Earth scientists! Today we are learning about the water cycle. The water cycle is the journey of water around our planet — it never stops! First, the sun heats the ocean and evaporation happens — water becomes vapor. Next, the vapor rises into the sky and condensation happens — it forms clouds. Then, the clouds get heavy and precipitation happens — rain or snow falls. Finally, the water flows back to rivers and the ocean, and the cycle begins again. Listen and label the four stages on your water cycle diagram!

listening_script.text: Good morning, class! I will now explain the complete water cycle in my presentation. First, evaporation happens when sunlight warms the surface of the ocean or a lake. Water molecules escape into the air as invisible water vapor. Next, condensation happens high in the atmosphere where the air is colder. The vapor forms tiny droplets that clump together and create clouds. Then, precipitation happens when the clouds become too heavy and water falls as rain. Finally, the water collects in rivers and oceans, and the cycle starts all over again — the same water has cycled on Earth for billions of years!
